summaryEn: In Kevin Rose's Foundation series, Musk talks at length about his childhood, learning by reading, starting companies, and his now-famous explanation of "first principles" reasoning — boiling problems down to fundamental truths rather than reasoning by analogy.
summaryZh: 在凯文·罗斯的《Foundation》系列节目中，马斯克详细谈到了自己的童年、通过阅读学习、创办公司，以及他如今广为人知的对“第一性原理”推理的解释——将问题归结为基本事实，而不是通过类比进行推理。

segments.textEn: Welcome to Foundation, a show where we profile some of the world's most interesting entrepreneurs. For more episodes, check out foundation kr. Today we're talking to Elon Musk, a founder at Tesla, SpaceX and PayPal. Let's go talk to him.
segments.textZh: 欢迎收看《Foundation》，这是一档介绍世界上一些最有意思的创业者的节目。想看更多期节目，请查看 foundation kr。今天我们要采访埃隆·马斯克，他是 Tesla、SpaceX 和 PayPal 的创始人。我们去和他聊聊吧。

segments.textEn: So let's start at the beginning. Where'd you grow up?
segments.textZh: 那么我们从头说起吧。你是在哪里长大的？

segments.textEn: I was born in South Africa, lived there till I was 17 and then moved by myself. Should I give you the whole story?
segments.textZh: 我出生在南非，在那里一直生活到17岁，然后独自搬走了。我要把整个故事都讲给你听吗？

segments.textEn: Yeah, I would love to hear the very beginning.
segments.textZh: 好啊，我很想听听最开始的事情。

segments.textEn: Sure. So yeah, I was born in Pretoria, South Africa, lived in Johannesburg, in Durban as well. Was able to travel to a few countries growing up within Africa and around the world. Went to the US when I was, I don't know, 10ish or something like that. And I read a lot of comics and books and stuff and always seems and stuff and things on technology and it always seemed like when there was cool technology or things happening, it was kind of in the United States.
segments.textZh: 当然。对，我出生在南非比勒陀利亚，住过约翰内斯堡，也住过德班。小时候有机会去非洲境内和世界各地的几个国家旅行。我大概10岁左右去了美国，我也不清楚，差不多就是那个年纪。我读了很多漫画、书之类的东西，而且总是看起来还有关于科技的东西和事情，而且似乎每当有什么很酷的技术或事情发生时，地点差不多都是美国。

segments.textEn: So my goal as a kid was to try to get to America basically.
segments.textZh: 所以我小时候的目标基本上就是设法去美国。

segments.textEn: What were your favorite comics?
segments.textZh: 你最喜欢哪些漫画？

segments.textEn: Well, I read every comic in the store.
segments.textZh: 嗯，店里的每一本漫画我都读过。

segments.textEn: I like obviously the Batman, Superman stuff, I mean, the Green Lantern, Iron Man. Gotta not say Iron man first because then people will think. But I did think that was a pretty cool one.
segments.textZh: 我当然喜欢蝙蝠侠、超人之类的，我是说，还有绿灯侠、钢铁侠。不能先说钢铁侠，因为那样人们就会觉得。不过我确实觉得那是个相当酷的角色。

segments.textEn: But I read everything like Doctor Strange.
segments.textZh: 但我什么都读，比如奇异博士。

segments.textEn: If there was a comic on the rack, I read it.
segments.textZh: 只要书架上有漫画，我就会读。

segments.textEn: Awesome. And when did you decide to get into computers and technology?
segments.textZh: 太棒了。那你是什么时候决定进入计算机和科技领域的？

segments.textEn: Did you start coding?
segments.textZh: 你开始写代码了吗？

segments.textEn: Or is it just a lot of noise, a lot of construction going on?
segments.textZh: 还是只是噪声很大，有很多施工正在进行？

segments.textEn: Can you still hear ok. Ok, we're good.
segments.textZh: 你还能听清吗。好，没问题。

segments.textEn: So did you start coding?
segments.textZh: 那么你开始写代码了吗？

segments.textEn: Yeah.
segments.textZh: 对。

segments.textEn: So when I was about 10 years old, I went into a store in South Africa and saw a Commodore Vic 20. And I guess maybe I was nine years old, I don't know, somewhere at that time. And I thought this was like the most awesome thing I'd ever seen. And you could make this, write computer programs and make games. And I played Atari and other things, other games, consoles, when I was like maybe six or seven. So the idea of being able to create games, that's always really exciting.
segments.textZh: 所以在我大约10岁时，我走进南非的一家商店，看到了一台 Commodore VIC-20。我想当时我也可能是9岁，我不知道，大概就是那个时候。我觉得这简直是我见过的最棒的东西。你可以让这个，编写计算机程序和制作游戏。我大概6岁或7岁时玩过雅达利和其他东西、其他游戏、游戏机。所以，能够创作游戏这个想法一直都非常令人兴奋。

segments.textEn: And so that was my first computer. It was a Commodore Vic 20. I think it had like 8k of memory.
segments.textZh: 所以那就是我的第一台电脑。是一台 Commodore VIC-20。我记得它好像有8k内存。

segments.textEn: And then what led you into entrepreneurship? Was it something that you always knew that you wanted to be an entrepreneur and start something on your own or did you stumble into it? Yeah,
segments.textZh: 那么，是什么促使你走上创业道路的？你是不是一直都知道自己想成为创业者、独自创办些什么，还是说你是偶然走上这条路的？对，

segments.textEn: I wouldn't say that. I always knew that I wanted to be an entrepreneur. I actually wasn't sure what I wanted to do growing up. And I think at one point I thought, well, Inventing stuff or creating things would be a cool thing to do, but I wasn't really sure if that meant starting a company or whether that meant working for a company that made cool stuff.
segments.textZh: 我不会这么说。我并非一直都知道自己想成为创业者。事实上，我小时候并不确定自己想做什么。我想有那么一段时间，我觉得，嗯，发明东西或创造事物会是一件很酷的事，但我并不确定那究竟意味着创办一家公司，还是去一家制造很酷东西的公司工作。

segments.textEn: And in fact, when I first came out to Silicon Valley, it was to do grad studies at Stanford in applied physics, material science. And then in 95, I kind of thought the Internet would be something that would change the world in a major way and I wanted to be part of it. And actually what I first tried to do was I tried to get a job at Netscape, so I wouldn't actually try to start a company. I tried to get a job at Netscape.
segments.textZh: 事实上，我最初来到硅谷，是为了在斯坦福大学攻读应用物理学、材料科学的研究生课程。后来在95年，我觉得互联网会成为一种以重大方式改变世界的事物，我想成为其中的一员。其实我最初尝试做的是去网景公司找份工作，所以我实际上并没有试图创办公司。我试过去网景公司找工作。

segments.textEn: And then that didn't work out. No, I didn't get any reply. So, I mean, I had a physics and economics degree or physics and business degree from Wharton, and I was doing grad studies in applied physics and science. And I guess that, you know, I didn't have a computer science degree or several years working at a software company.
segments.textZh: 然后那件事没成。不，我没有收到任何回复。所以，我是说，我有物理学和经济学学位，或者说沃顿商学院的物理学和商科学位，而且当时正在攻读应用物理学和科学的研究生课程。我想，你知道，我没有计算机科学学位，也没有在软件公司工作数年的经历。

segments.textEn: Well, so for whatever reason, I didn't get a reply from Netscape. And I actually tried hanging out in the lobby, but I was. I was too shy to talk to anyone. So I was just like standing in the lobby and I. And then I just walk in.
segments.textZh: 嗯，所以不管出于什么原因，我没有收到网景公司的回复。实际上我还试过在大堂里待着，但我当时。我太害羞了，不敢和任何人说话。所以我就那样站在大堂里，然后我。然后我就走进去。

segments.textEn: Did you have your resume with you or was it.
segments.textZh: 你当时带着简历吗，还是说。

segments.textEn: Yeah, actually it was pretty embarrassing. I was just sort of standing there trying to see if there's someone I could talk to and then I just couldn't. I couldn't. I was too scared to talk to anyone. So then I left. Amazing.
segments.textZh: 对，其实那相当尴尬。我就只是站在那里，试着看看有没有人可以和我谈谈，然后我就是做不到。我做不到。我太害怕了，不敢和任何人说话。所以后来我就离开了。太不可思议了。

segments.textEn: So then you went on to do what from that point?
segments.textZh: 那么从那时起，你接下来去做了什么？

segments.textEn: So then I just. I was just writing software that summer and it got to the start of the quarter for Stanford and I had to make a decision, so I decided to go on deferment. So I figure if I start a company and it doesn't work, then I can always go back to grad school. It's just, you know. So I talked to the chairman of the department and he let me go on deferment. And I said I'll probably be back in six months. And he said he's probably never going to hear from me again.
segments.textZh: 然后我就只是。我那个夏天一直在写软件，等到斯坦福大学的学季开始时，我必须作出决定，所以我决定申请延期入学。我想，如果我创办一家公司但没有成功，那我随时可以回去读研究生。就是，你知道。所以我和系主任谈了谈，他允许我延期入学。我说我大概6个月后就会回来。他说他可能再也不会收到我的消息了。

segments.textEn: And he was correct. I've never spoken to him since.
segments.textZh: 他说对了。从那以后，我再也没有和他说过话。

segments.textEn: So.
segments.textZh: 所以。

segments.textEn: Yeah, so started company with my brother and a friend of mine, Greg Curry, and the three of us created Zip2, which, where the initial idea was to create software that could help bring the media companies online. So we helped in a small way bring companies like New York Times, Hearst Niter and so forth, bring them online. They weren't actually always online. People don't realize that.
segments.textZh: 是的，所以我和我兄弟，还有我的一个朋友格雷格·柯里一起创办了公司，我们3个人创建了 Zip2，最初的想法是开发能帮助媒体公司上线的软件。所以我们以微薄之力帮助《纽约时报》、Hearst Niter 等公司上线。它们其实并非一直都在线。人们没有意识到这一点。

segments.textEn: Were you the CEO at the time or did you give that role to someone else?
segments.textZh: 当时你是首席执行官，还是把这个职位交给了别人？

segments.textEn: Yeah, I started off being the CEO. So I was CEO for probably the first year and then.
segments.textZh: 是的，我一开始担任首席执行官。所以我大概在第一年担任首席执行官，然后。

segments.textEn: But after we got VC funding, the veg capitalist wanted to hire a professional CEO.
segments.textZh: 但在我们获得风险投资后，那个蔬菜资本家想聘请一位职业首席执行官。

segments.textEn: Was that frustrating or were you like, this is over my head. I'm ready to give up this role to someone else.
segments.textZh: 那让你感到沮丧吗，还是你当时觉得，这超出了我的能力范围。我准备把这个职位交给别人。

segments.textEn: At the time I thought it was a good idea because I didn't really know what I was doing. And I figured they would hire someone who would be really good and that person would increase the chances of success of the company. And so that seemed like a good thing. And then I could work on software and kind of product direction and that's what I like doing. So that seemed like a great thing. Now, in retrospect, I think that wasn't the best thing because the person that was hired, in my opinion, was actually not that great.
segments.textZh: 当时我觉得这是个好主意，因为我确实不知道自己在做什么。而且我以为他们会聘请一个真正出色的人，那个人会提高公司成功的可能性。所以那似乎是件好事。然后我就可以从事软件和某种产品方向方面的工作，而那正是我喜欢做的。所以那似乎是件很棒的事。现在回过头看，我认为那并不是最好的做法，因为在我看来，受聘的那个人其实没有那么出色。

segments.textEn: So I think, yeah, I mean, I think quite frankly, the company succeeded in spite of that person, not because of them.
segments.textZh: 所以我想，是的，我是说，坦率地说，我认为公司是在那个人的妨碍下取得成功的，而不是因为那个人。

segments.textEn: You know, starting a company for the first time is very challenging for a lot of people. They don't even know where to begin. You must have run into a lot of. I mean, we all made mistakes in starting our first company. As far as hiring, like you said, the people you bring in, like CEO that replaced you, did you surround yourself with mentors? How did you. Who did you look to for advice?
segments.textZh: 你知道，第一次创办公司对很多人来说都非常具有挑战性。他们甚至不知道该从何着手。你肯定遇到过很多。我是说，我们第一次创业时都犯过错误。就招聘而言，就像你说的，你招进来的人，比如接替你的首席执行官，你有没有让导师围绕在自己身边？你是怎么。你会向谁寻求建议？

segments.textEn: I read a lot of books and talked to lots of people. I didn't have any one person who was a mentor, but I always look for feedback from people around me and feedback from an historical context, which is books, basically. So that's.
segments.textZh: 我读了很多书，也和很多人交谈过。我没有某一个具体的人作为导师，但我总是寻求周围人的反馈，也从历史背景中寻求反馈，基本上就是通过书籍。所以就是这样。

segments.textEn: Any books stand out as something that was something that you really relied upon. Well, are they just general business books or.
segments.textZh: 有没有什么书特别突出，是你真正依赖的。嗯，它们只是一般的商业书籍，还是。

segments.textEn: I didn't read actually very many general business books, but I like biographies and autobiographies. I think those are pretty helpful.
segments.textZh: 其实我没有读过很多一般的商业书籍，但我喜欢传记和自传。我认为这些书相当有帮助。

segments.textEn: So I like. And actually some aren't really business, although, like something like Franklin's, both his autobiography and say the biography that's recently been written by. Or not that recently, but In, I guess five or 10 years ago, whenever it was written. The biography of Bon Isaacson on Franklin is really good. You can sort of see how he kind of. Because he was an entrepreneur. I mean, he sort of started from nothing, actually was just like a runaway kid basically and created his printing business and sort of how he went about doing that.
segments.textZh: 所以我喜欢。而且实际上有些并不算真正的商业书籍，不过，比如富兰克林的书，包括他的自传，以及比如最近由。或者也不是那么近，但我猜是在5年或10年前写的，不管具体是什么时候写的。邦·艾萨克森写的富兰克林传记非常好。你多少能看出他是怎样有点。因为他是一位企业家。我是说，他算是白手起家，实际上基本就是一个离家出走的孩子，然后创办了自己的印刷企业，以及他大致是如何着手做这件事的。

segments.textEn: And then over time he also did science and politics. Other. I would say certainly he's one of the people I most admire. Franklin's pretty awesome. But then I think it's also worth reading books on scientists and engineers. Tesla obviously.
segments.textZh: 然后随着时间推移，他也从事科学和政治。其他。我会说，他当然是我最敬佩的人之一。富兰克林非常了不起。不过我认为，关于科学家和工程师的书也值得一读。Tesla，显然。

segments.textEn: Did you hear about that Tesla museum that they're having built now?
segments.textZh: 你听说过他们现在正在建造的那座 Tesla 博物馆吗？

segments.textEn: I actually contributed some funding to save the land.
segments.textZh: 实际上我出了一些资金来保住那块土地。

segments.textEn: Oh, that's great. Awesome. That was a very cool thing that Oatmeal did.
segments.textZh: 哦，那太好了。真棒。Oatmeal 做的那件事非常酷。

segments.textEn: Yeah, it was pretty cool. I like the way that they put it too. It's like, let's have a goddamn Tesla museum.
segments.textZh: 是的，相当酷。我也喜欢他们表达这件事的方式。就像是，让我们建一座该死的 Tesla 博物馆。

segments.textEn: So fast forward a little bit. You know, you obviously did PayPal, that was very successful. And then at some point in time you're like, I'm gonna do something crazy, something that's never been done before with Tesla and the space related stuff you're into. I mean, why take on such huge, very ambitious type projects? I mean, did you have ever have a feeling like this might not work?
segments.textZh: 那么稍微快进一点。你知道，你显然做了 PayPal，而且非常成功。然后在某个时刻，你就像是，我要做一件疯狂的事，一件以前从未有人做过的事，也就是 Tesla 和你所涉足的太空相关事务。我是说，为什么要承担如此庞大、如此雄心勃勃的项目？我是说，你是否曾经觉得，这可能行不通？

segments.textEn: Oh yeah, absolutely. Well, so this kind of goes back to college where I was trying to figure out what are the things that would most affect the future of humanity. And the things that I thought would most affect the future would be the Internet sustainable energy, which is both production and consumption. And so effectively solar cities like production, Tesla's consumption in a sustainable way, and then also space exploration and specifically making life multi planetary.
segments.textZh: 哦，是的，当然。嗯，这得追溯到大学时期，当时我试图弄清楚，哪些事物会对人类的未来产生最大影响。而我认为会对未来产生最大影响的事物是互联网、可持续能源，其中既包括生产也包括消费。所以实际上，像太阳城是生产，Tesla 是以可持续方式进行消费，然后还有太空探索，尤其是让生命成为多行星生命。

segments.textEn: Now I didn't expect at the time to be involved in all those areas, but those are just the areas that I thought would most affect the future. And as it turned out, I've been fortunate enough to be involved in those areas, but that's the thread that connects them. It's like it's kind of my best guess at what would most likely affect the future in the biggest way.
segments.textZh: 当时我并没料到自己会参与所有这些领域，但它们就是我认为会对未来产生最大影响的领域。事实证明，我足够幸运，能够参与这些领域，而这就是将它们串联起来的主线。就像是，这算是我对什么最有可能以最大的方式影响未来所作出的最佳猜测。

segments.textEn: And when I first thought about doing something in space, the thing I was going to do was actually going to be a philanthropic mission to Mars to land a small greenhouse on the surface of Mars with seeds and dehydrated nutrient gel that you'd hydrate upon landing. You'd have this little greenhouse on Mars and you have this great shot of green plants on the red background. And the public tends to respond to precedents and superlatives.
segments.textZh: 当我最初考虑在太空领域做些什么时，我原本真正打算做的是一项前往火星的慈善任务，把一座小型温室降落在火星表面，里面装着种子和脱水营养凝胶，着陆后再给它补水。这样火星上就会有这座小温室，你还能拍到一张很棒的照片，红色背景上是绿色植物。而公众往往会对首创之举和创纪录的事物作出反应。

segments.textEn: I thought that would get people really excited about sending life to Mars. And my expectation from that project would be 100% loss because I wouldn't expect, maybe you can make a little bit back on advertising or sponsorship or something, but it would be essentially a complete loss. So starting a rocket company would necessarily have a greater likely outcome than 0% financial return.
segments.textZh: 我以为那会让人们对把生命送往火星感到非常兴奋。而我对那个项目的预期会是100%的损失，因为我不会指望，也许可以从广告、赞助或其他什么上收回一点钱，但它基本上会是彻底的损失。所以，创办一家火箭公司的财务回报至少更有可能高于0%。

segments.textEn: But at the beginning of starting SpaceX, I thought that the most likely Outcome was failure.
segments.textZh: 但在创办 SpaceX 之初，我认为最有可能的结果是失败。

segments.textEn: And how about Tesla Motors? Walk me through your process of wanting to launch something like that.
segments.textZh: 那Tesla Motors呢？给我讲讲你想创办这样一家公司的过程。

segments.textEn: Yeah. So in terms of an electric car company, at first I thought that there would be no need to do an electric car company startup because California regulations basically forced General Motors to create the Volt, or rather the EV1, I should say. So when General Motors had the EV1, I thought, hey, this is great. Biggest car company in the world is making electric car called the EV1. That would imply that there's going to be an EV2, 3, 4.
segments.textZh: 是的。所以就电动汽车公司而言，一开始我认为没有必要创办一家电动汽车初创公司，因为加州的法规基本上迫使通用汽车制造了Volt，或者更确切地说，我应该说是EV1。所以当通用汽车推出EV1时，我想，嘿，这太棒了。世界上最大的汽车公司正在制造一款名为EV1的电动汽车。那意味着接下来会有EV2、3、4。

segments.textEn: They killed that project off though, right?
segments.textZh: 不过他们把那个项目终止了，对吧？

segments.textEn: They did, yeah. And that was very unwise.
segments.textZh: 他们确实这么做了，是的。而且那非常不明智。

segments.textEn: I mean it's sort of really short sighted, I think. Action. I mean in retrospect that seems perhaps obvious, but at the time, not only did they cancel the project, they forcibly removed the EV ones that they'd given out, which they only gave out on lease. They removed them from customers against their wishes, took the cars and crushed them in a yard so that they could never be used again.

segments.textZh: 至于电池，他们会说，哦，它要花费。你知道，历史上它的成本是每……600美元。每千瓦时600美元。所以未来也不会比这好多少。而你会说，不，好吧，电池是由什么制成的？所以从第一性原理出发，就是要问，好吧，电池由哪些材料成分构成？这些材料成分在现货市场上的价值是多少？所以你可以说，好吧，它含有钴、镍、铝、碳，以及一些用于分隔的聚合物。

segments.textEn: And a seal can. So break that down on a material basis and say, okay, if we bought that in London Metal Exchange, what would each of those things cost? segments.textZh: 还有一个密封罐。所以从材料层面把它拆解开来，然后问，好吧，如果我们在伦敦金属交易所购买这些材料，每一种要花多少钱？就像，哦，天哪，大约是每千瓦时80美元。所以显然，你只需要想出巧妙的办法，把这些材料组合成电池单元的形状，这样你就能造出比任何人意识到的都要便宜得多、便宜得多的电池。
